nameStory: African lovegrass earned its 'weeping' nickname from its graceful, drooping seed heads that bend and sway in the breeze like tears. The 'love' in lovegrass comes from the delicate, airy appearance of the seed clusters that seem to float like romantic whispers in the wind. Its African heritage reflects its origins in southern Africa, though it has traveled far from home to establish itself in New England.
description: African lovegrass is a clumping perennial grass that forms dense tufts of narrow, arching leaves. It typically grows 2-4 feet tall and wide, creating fountain-like mounds of blue-green to grayish foliage. In late summer, it produces distinctive drooping seed heads that give the plant its weeping appearance. This non-native grass has established small populations in New England, though it remains relatively uncommon in our region.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms dense, fountain-like clumps with arching leaves that curve gracefully outward and downward, creating a distinctive weeping or cascading appearance

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, thread-like leaves that feel smooth to the touch and range from blue-green to grayish in color, growing in tight bunches from the base

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Produces airy, drooping seed heads on tall stems in late summer that feel papery when mature and dance gracefully in even light breezes

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Tiny seeds arranged in delicate, cloud-like clusters that remain attached to the drooping branches, creating a misty appearance

habitat: In New England, African lovegrass is occasionally found in disturbed areas, roadsides, and waste places, particularly in well-drained soils. It prefers sunny, open locations and can tolerate poor, dry conditions. Look for it in areas where ornamental plantings may have escaped cultivation or where seeds have been inadvertently introduced.

seasonality.spring: New green growth emerges from the base of established clumps, with fresh leaves appearing bright green before developing their characteristic blue-gray tint.
seasonality.summer: Reaches full size with mature foliage displaying the典型 fountain-like growth habit. Seed heads begin developing in late summer.
seasonality.fall: Distinctive drooping seed heads are most prominent and identifiable, turning golden-brown and persisting on the plant through early fall.
seasonality.winter: Foliage turns tan to brown but often remains partially evergreen in milder winters, with dried seed heads sometimes persisting.

funFact: African lovegrass was originally introduced to North America as an ornamental plant and for erosion control, but it has such strong roots that it can survive being completely buried by sand dunes and still grow back through several feet of sand!
confusionNotes: African lovegrass can be confused with other ornamental fountain grasses, but its distinctly drooping (weeping) seed heads and blue-gray foliage set it apart from most natives. Remember: if it looks like it's crying graceful tears, it's likely weeping lovegrass.
contextualKnowledge: Though called 'African' lovegrass, it's also known by several other common names including weeping lovegrass and Boer lovegrass, which can cause confusion when trying to identify it. The name 'Boer' refers to its origins in South Africa, where it was valued by early Dutch settlers.
compareHints: African lovegrass differs from other New England lovegrasses by its distinctive weeping growth habit and blue-gray foliage color. Purple lovegrass has more upright seed heads with purplish tints, while little lovegrass forms much smaller, less dramatic clumps. The drooping, fountain-like appearance of African lovegrass is unique among our regional lovegrasses.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Purple Lovegrass is the showiest of New England's lovegrasses, with much larger and more colorful flower clusters than its relatives like Little Lovegrass or Teal Lovegrass.
Among New England's lovegrasses, purple lovegrass is distinguished by its compact, tufted growth habit and relatively small size.

Teal lovegrass stands out from its lovegrass relatives primarily by its wetland habitat - while purple lovegrass, little lovegrass, and most others prefer dry, disturbed soils, teal lovegrass is the water-lover of the family.
Among the lovegrasses in New England, Little Lovegrass is one of the smallest and most delicate-looking.
Among New England's love-grasses, Jersey Love-grass is the most delicate and airy-looking.
Tiny lovegrass lives up to its name by being much smaller and more delicate than its lovegrass relatives like purple lovegrass, which forms more substantial clumps.

Among the lovegrasses, Frank's Lovegrass sits in the middle size-wise—larger than Tiny Lovegrass with its hair-thin appearance, but smaller and less showy than Purple Lovegrass which often forms more substantial clumps.
